title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
description: Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Vol
body: Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause."We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue."This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h). This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step."We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing."Earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing."I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response.A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park café in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity".

schema.headline: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC

title: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
description: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donal
body: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump."The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship. "Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote."If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her -  or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated."Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC. "The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe." Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation". But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago. Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

schema.headline: Obama blasts Trump administration probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'

title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, authorities say
description: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local aut
body: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

schema.headline: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, authorities say

title: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and t
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place.In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.The woman told the Southwark Crown Court jury the "lad culture" of the 2000s stopped her from reporting the TV star.She has accused Brand of grabbing her breasts at the bar in Soho in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet and allegedly raping her.The pair had been attending a birthday party when the alleged incidents happened.She said she waited two decades to come forward to the police because the thought of doing so "terrified" her.She said his celebrity status meant "it would be his word against mine"."I would be ostracised in my work environment or friends."The complainant worked for MTV at the time and said she was often surrounded by famous people.From behind a blue screen in the witness box she said times had changed.In those days - she said - "you weren't believed as a woman and it was a lad culture of 'you wearing this, so you were asking for it' and all that rubbish you were told back then".The complainant recalled Brand's "big weird grin" which she compared to the face of a clown as he allegedly launched forward and grabbed hold of her.Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested during cross examination that Brand and the woman went to the toilet consensually for a "kiss and a cuddle", but they abandoned the attempt to have a sexual encounter because of the filthy state of the flooded toilet.The woman, who became tearful while giving evidence, has rejected this version of events.She said she felt "dazed" after the alleged attack.Pressed on her claim of being dragged into the toilets against her will, the defendant's barrister suggested it would have been "perfectly easy" for her to have struggled or asked for help.She said she did not agree because he had been holding her quite strongly, saying "part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".She described feeling numb and ashamed afterwards.She told the jury she had later confided in a friend, telling them Brand had  "tried to do it" - but held back from saying he had "succeeded" in raping her.The woman told the prosecution barrister that she didn't even know at the time that the alleged oral attack would be legally considered as rape.Earlier on Monday, the jury was shown a 2023 video interview with an officer in which the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.In her recorded interview with police, the woman said "he literally just grabbed my boobs out of nowhere in the middle of the conversation, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs".A short while later, she said he "dragged me in the toilets" where the floor was flooded, before "he unzipped himself" and allegedly orally raped her.She said the alleged rape was "swift", and left her "in disbelief and shock"."The toilets were behind where he stood. It was literally just grab and pull. He was holding me quite strongly on the arm and pulled me in that direction," she said."Part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here"."I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there. I just remember it felt like a force. I definitely said I don't want to do this," she added.After the alleged rape, the woman, who was in her 20s at the time, said Brand "turned to me and said 'oh I guess we should swap numbers now', like it was just all normal, like he hadn't just forced me to do that."Brand denies all the charges he faces.He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

schema.headline: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape

title: Tennis star Svitolina says emotional toll of Ukraine war led to Monfils separation
description: Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player Gaël Monfils, citing the emotional impact
body: Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player Gaël Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country.The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside". "This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage.She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget". "Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote.It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said."Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said. Ukraine's Black Sea port city has been heavily bombed by Russia throughout the war.Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022."What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself."The tennis power couple married in 2021 and have one child together - a four-year-old daughter called Skai.Svitolina said her daughter "will always come first", adding "our marriage is ending, but our family is not".Monfils, a former world number six, was expected to play the final tournament of his career at next month's Paris Masters in an emotional farewell.However, the two-time Grand Slam semi-finalist's retirement was effectively confirmed last week when he appeared on the International Tennis Integrity Authority's list of retired players.Once a player removes themselves from anti-doping protocols, they are not eligible to compete in professional tournaments.Monfils, who won 13 titles on the ATP Tour, is preparing to start a new career in finance after joining a Swiss wealth management firm.

schema.headline: Tennis star Svitolina says emotional toll of Ukraine war led to Monfils separation

title: Crystal Palace: Manager Pierre Sage facing a fight to keep his job
description: While no-one doubted that following in Oliver Glasner's footsteps as Crystal Palace manager would be a difficult task, Pierre Sage now finds his posit
body: While no-one doubted that following in Oliver Glasner's footsteps as Crystal Palace manager would be a difficult task, Pierre Sage now finds his position under close scrutiny. A string of poor results - most recently Sunday's 5-0 drubbing by Brighton - makes this week a crucial one in determining his future.Sage has won just two of his opening seven Premier League games in charge, while the 17 goals they have conceded is the most in the league.But there is a degree of sympathy from some behind the scenes at Selhurst Park that the Frenchman has been dealt a difficult hand.Injuries have not been kind, while the absence of Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr - due to a mixture of fitness and personal issues, related to both players' desire to leave the club - has not helped the start of his reign.Co-owner and chairman Steve Parish is not one to act on impulse. He resisted the temptation to act when Glasner publicly criticised the club's board for "abandoning" the team after the decision to sell Marc Guehi to Manchester City in January.Glasner saw out his contract and added the Europa Conference League title to the FA Cup won the season before.Not that Sage is out of the woods. With crucial games against Besiktas and Newcastle on the horizon, further poor results will leave Parish with a decision to make.Some figures close to Palace believe the writing is already on the wall and, when the right replacement is in place, his short tenure will come to an end.But, having failed to appoint first-choice target Andoni Iraola following Glasner's exit, Palace are well aware of the difficulties of the managerial market.What is for sure is that the 47-year-old is facing a fight to keep his job.Sage may point to the disbanding of the squad that led Palace to their first ever major trophies, with the FA Cup in 2025 before last season's Europa Conference League triumph, as the reason for his tough start to life in south London.Eberechi Eze, Michael Olise, Maxence Lacroix, Daniel Munoz and Guehi have all departed Selhurst Park since the summer of 2024.The departure of highly influential sporting director Dougie Freedman in 2025 has also been keenly felt.In addition to Sage, the position of Freedman's replacement Matt Hobbs is also under the spotlight.But conceding 17 goals in seven Premier League matches points to a problem, at least in part, of Sage's own making.The team's recent DNA is rooted in defensive stability. Predecessors Glasner and Roy Hodgson produced well-organised teams with a solid base for its attacking players.Conceding close to 2.5 goals per game is so far removed from what the team's recent successes has been built upon that it has raised major concern from the club's powerbrokers.Palace are currently on course to concede 92 goals this season. No club has conceded more since Sheffield United shipped 104 goals to finish bottom in 2024. Personnel is contributing to those defensive deficiencies. Losing Guehi, Lacroix and Munoz in the space of six months represent significant losses.From the three centre-backs that started in Sunday's 5-0 loss to Brighton, Jaydee Canvot is 20 years old and Honest Ahanor only 18.Nevertheless, there is a clear sense from inside the club that Sage's system and approach has been a major contributing factor towards their troubles in defence.There is a perception from sections of supporters that the club's summer defensive recruitment has not helped.Takehiro Tomiyasu, Ben Chilwell and Oscar Mingueza arrived on free transfers, while Axel Disasi and Ahanor arrived on loan.As mitigation, it is understood Palace have encountered major difficulty in complying with Uefa's financial rules, leaving them hampered in the transfer market.Trying to stay within Uefa's guidelines was among the reasons why the club sold Munoz to Nottingham Forest for £22m.But those financial difficulties do not make the situation Sage finds himself any less critical.With a Europa League trip to Besiktas and home Premier League game against Newcastle on the horizon, Sage has an opportunity to change the mood music.Two positive results and the Frenchman will hope he can mount a more consistent upward trend.Two defeats, however, and Palace may well feel that enough is enough.

schema.headline: Crystal Palace: Manager Pierre Sage facing a fight to keep his job

title: Spurs 3-1 Coventry: James Maddison shines on Tottenham return
description: Roberto de Zerbi has used all the tools at his disposal to discover the missing spark in struggling Tottenham Hotspur, from acting as an amateur psych
body: Roberto de Zerbi has used all the tools at his disposal to discover the missing spark in struggling Tottenham Hotspur, from acting as an amateur psychologist to team bonding dinners, then a sunshine break in Marbella.The answer, at least when Spurs finally moved off the bottom of the table with their first Premier League win this season against Coventry City, came in the shape of James Maddison as he made his first start in 18 months.He missed most of last season after suffering an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in pre-season, before fracturing his shoulder in the opening-weekend defeat at Brentford in this campaign.The 29-year-old finally made it back into the Spurs starting line-up to face Coventry - and delivered in spectacular style to set them on the way to a 3-1 victory that De Zerbi hopes will finally give their season lift-off.Maddison could barely keep the smile from his face as he warmed up, then made his mark in the 14th minute by showing what Spurs have been missing with a brilliant right-foot finish from 20 yards, taking Mohammed Kudus' pass first time to arc a sweeping strike high beyond Coventry City keeper Carl Rushworth.It was a moment of sweet relief for Maddison, the goal getting loud gasps of admiration from Spurs supporters as it was shown several times on the stadium's big screens.Even though the goal came against his former club, Maddison celebrated with his trademark imaginary dart throwing motion before kissing the badge on his Spurs shirt.Maddison's significance to Spurs is illustrated by the fact they had won just 12 out of 57 Premier League games since his last top-flight goal, in a 1-0 victory against Manchester United in February 2025. They had averaged less than a point a game since then.And since his last start, at Liverpool on 27 April 2025, Spurs had won only 11 of 49 league games in between, losing 23.Spurs cannot kid themselves that this was a glorious victory. It was actually only their sixth win in the past 37 home league games - drawing 10 and losing 21 - and just their fourth league victory overall in 2026, having played 27, drawn 10 and lost 13.And it was the first time they scored three goals or more at home in the league since the opening day of last season, when they beat Burnley 3-0 in Thomas Frank's first game in charge.There are still too many nerves around Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and in De Zerbi's team for calm and relaxation.The victory margin flattered them somewhat, with Jack Rudoni equalising for Coventry City before Omar Marmoush's strike for his first goal for the club, then another from Ben Davies in stoppage time after a dreadful Rushworth error finally allowed Spurs to enjoy the relief of victory.And there were other things to celebrate. As well as Maddison's successful return to the starting line-up, there was the sight of Dejan Kulusevski finally back as an 87th-minute replacement for Kudus after 526 days out with a knee injury.Maddison got a deserved standing ovation when he was substituted for Conor Gallagher after 69 minutes, but the reception for Kulusevski was arguably even more rapturous as he finally took to the pitch again after such a long battle to regain fitness.It was Maddison, however, who claimed the major plaudits after he was the driving force behind the win that has proved so elusive - his positive approach playing with a smile on his face provides refreshment of its own after such a depressing sequence of results.He was eager to get on the ball, was constantly probing and prompting, all before he inevitably tired after the break."I spoke to the gaffer this weekend about it, feeling like it was the right moment for me to go back into the starting XI after a bit of a stop-start start to the season," Maddison told Sky Sports."I just wanted to play well and show my abilities, show what the team has missed the last 18 months. The gaffer asked me to play and wanted to enjoy watching from the side. Hopefully I did that, and a goal is always nice."If his aim was to show what Spurs have been missing, this was very much mission accomplished.And as well as Maddison and Kulusevski, Marmoush will gain confidence from his strike, another superb curling effort that gave Rushworth no chance.De Zerbi will know this is only a start, with a tough trip to face Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday evening (17:30 BST).He welcomed the return of Maddison and Kulusevski, saying: "They are different players, different talents, different personalities. With them in the dressing room there is a different atmosphere."What changes the atmosphere in the dressing room and beyond most are victories.Now De Zerbi and Spurs can actually build on three points at last, and the sights of Maddison and Kulusevski back in action will have the Italian hoping they can accelerate an improvement after the misery of recent times.

schema.headline: Spurs 3-1 Coventry: James Maddison shines on Tottenham return

title: Sarina Wiegman contract: Why England manager faces biggest challenge yet
description: Wiegman's successful England teams have been built on a core group of players from an outstanding generation - but a few cracks have appeared this yea
body: Wiegman's successful England teams have been built on a core group of players from an outstanding generation - but a few cracks have appeared this year.Seven of the team that started against world champions Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - and their 4-0 defeat in Mallorca laid bare the gap England must bridge to the world's best.That result also consigned England to two rounds of play-offs to reach next summer's World Cup.Beating Greece this month navigated the first of those, with games against Ukraine, who they have beaten twice already in 2026, to come before Christmas.Nevertheless, finding successors to those who have spearheaded the success will not be straightforward.Defensive stalwarts Lucy Bronze and Alex Greenwood will be 37 and 36 respectively by Euro 2029, while Leah Williamson and Keira Walsh will be 32.Other key players such as Alessia Russo and Georgia Stanway will also have turned 30, far from past their best, but still a consideration."We have to continue the evolution of the Lionesses," record goalscorer Ellen White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast. "We can't stay stagnant or keep trying to win in the same ways all the time."Former England goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis thinks one of Wiegman's strengths as a manager is her willingness to give young players a chance. "She's not afraid of bringing in players who have never been capped before," Brown-Finnis told BBC Radio 5 Live. "Wiegman is looking right across the spectrum and asking who's on form, who can add to my squad, who can fill a position or a couple of different positions?" Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live's Monday Night Club, former Lionesses captain Steph Houghton said: "You can see Wiegman is trying to change a few things. The last camp she brought on Lexi Potter for her debut and she is now starting regularly for Chelsea. As a young player you need that to thrive in this environment."She is seeing the progress of young players coming through to press those who have been in the squad for a long time."It is not as though Wiegman has ignored squad regeneration.During her time in charge, she has handed debuts to 24 players, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters.Those games against Greece offered a clue to her next steps.In Crete, Manchester City's Laura Blindkilde Brown, 23, showed glimpses of her ball-playing ability, while in the second leg 20-year-old Chelsea academy graduate Potter impressed in midfield.London City's Freya Godfrey, 21, and talented 18-year-old Erica Meg Parkinson also got their first caps as Wiegman scrutinised her options.Figures earlier this season showed the number of homegrown starters has been dropping in the Women's Super League (WSL) over the past four campaigns, with the league's growing prestige attracting more foreign stars.The Football Association (FA) chief football officer Dan Ashworth said Wiegman has helped bring "a golden age for women's football in this country".To prolong it, she will need to keep producing fruit from increasingly arid ground.Prior to Wiegman's appointment, England women had performed well at major tournaments - finishing third at the World Cup in 2015 and fourth in 2019 - but winning Euro 2022 was something new.WSL attendances rocketed, media coverage surged and clubs amplified their women's teams. However, four years on, there is evidence to suggest interest has plateaued.Initial crowd figures for the 2026-27 season are down on previous campaigns, while only 18,587 fans watched England beat Greece 5-0 at King Power Stadium, nearly 10,000 fewer than qualifiers at Nottingham Forest's City Ground and Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium this year.With so much competition, Lionesses success is crucial for sustaining momentum in the women's game - but expectations are higher now.A fanbase was born from success and has become accustomed to it. Will they tolerate anything less than finals and trophies?After all, Spain, Japan and hosts Brazil are among the many nations that look poised to have a significant say at the World Cup next summer.

schema.headline: Sarina Wiegman contract: Why England manager faces biggest challenge yet

title: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya
description: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.Mackenzie ordered me
body: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows". Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings". Those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus", the judge said.One witness stated that a pregnant woman had been barred from nursing her new-born baby, who died 12 days later. "She was instructed to fast to death and follow her children," the witness said.Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children. But this is the first time the pastor has faced a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.He was arrested in 2023, after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie had led his followers from across the country.Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie."I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court."All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said ahead of the verdict, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day."Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old.""We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another." Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town. "We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside."The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him. Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him". When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned."My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said.The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said.By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers.Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest. He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover."My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said."I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest."Many of the bodies are still unidentified owing to their advanced state of decomposition. In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me". "Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said before the verdict was announced."I still love him and he is still my pastor."In contrast Dan Mackenzie believed his father should be found guilty of murder."He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing," also speaking before the verdict.

schema.headline: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya

title: The Simpsons: Apu returns with new voice after race row
description: The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes.Apu Nahas
body: The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes.Apu Nahasapeemapetilon - to give the much-loved shopkeeper his full name - re-appeared in Sunday's episode on US network Fox, titled The Revengening, but now voiced by India-born, US-raised actor Sunil Malhotra.The character has been seen but not heard around Springfield since the October 2017 episode The Serfsons, and his big return to action had reportedly been a closely guarded secret.Malhotra said in a statement posted on Instagram that it feels like a reclamation. "It truly is his homecoming," he said.The character, who has been part of the long-running American animation series since 1990, was previously voiced by a white actor, Hank Azaria, putting on a heavy Indian accent.Indian-American comic Hari Kondabolu made a documentary in 2017, titled the Problem With Apu, saying the character - a South Asian convenience store clerk - was founded on racial stereotypes.The Simpsons' Apu: 'A stereotype hiding in plain sight'The following year, an episode of The Simpsons addressed the controversy surrounding the Indian character for the first time, making a nod to the accusations but some viewers found it insufficient.Others defended the show and said all its characters were stereotypes.Azaria first announced he was stepping down from the role in 2020, and he later told Dax Shepherd's Armchair Expert podcast: "Part of me feels like I need to go around to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologise."Speaking to Variety, external ahead of the weekend's latest episode, Azaria's replacement Malhotra explained: "When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink."But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking: Did the writers' room look different now?"The Grey's Anatomy and The Legend of Korra actor continued: "Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologised for past mistakes?"Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably Simpsons way that didn't disappoint fans?"After years of Apu having become a mere background character, Malhotra said he spoke with showrunner Matt Selman and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos about how they could make the returning fans' favourite more culturally appropriate for 2026."It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for long-time fans of The Simpsons and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way."Apu's wife, Manjula, will now be voiced Janina Gavankar - who previously appeared in Apple TV's The Morning Show - taking over from Jan Hooks and Tress MacNeille.In Apu's haunting comeback episode, a man in a "Daft Monk" Halloween costume - a play on French electro duo Daft Punk - appears to be accidentally killed over and over again by Springfield residents.A year on he returns to wreak his revenge.Eventually he summons everyone to the Springfield City Hall, takes off his helmet and reveals himself to be Apu.He then shares his story of having been nearly killed dozens of times, before winding up on The Island of Forgotten Garbage, where he was healed by Dr Nick."I am the man you left for dead. I am the one you pretended never existed," he declares.Just as he is about to set the city hall ablaze, Marge Simpson - serving as a thinly-veiled mouthpiece for the producers - intervenes, telling him: "Apu, we're so sorry we left you for dead. Believe me, we wanted to do the right thing."Her famous bratty son Bart adds: "But we were so scared, and just didn't know what to do."Bart's father Homer then offers to sacrifice himself to save the rest of the town, reminding viewers of how important Apu has been to the town."You were on our bowling teams, our barbershop quartets, our dad rock cover bands," said Homer."We took you for granted. I took you for granted."The episode will be made available for viewers in the UK to watch on Disney+ next week.

schema.headline: The Simpsons: Apu returns with new voice after race row

title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
description: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, tha
body: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland. Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks  on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024. It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with UkraineIvan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome."At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets."When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance."You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets."This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live."In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals."As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."But he argued that his team's actions were justified."I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.Foma did his own digging on Ivan.After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident. Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too."The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.Foma has the same rule for his operatives."As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work."Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him."You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag."There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work."Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change."Putin won't live forever," he said.

schema.headline: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia

title: Gianni Infantino: Uefa gives Fifa deadline to release key documents
description: European governing body Uefa has told Fifa it must release key documents and answer all questions relating to its governance and decision-making by a
body: European governing body Uefa has told Fifa it must release key documents and answer all questions relating to its governance and decision-making by a deadline of 2 November.At the Fifa Council on Thursday, president Gianni Infantino apologised for his World Cup sell-off plan - but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised. In the letter seen by BBC Sport, Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis said that world football's governing body had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions"."Others remain unanswered, and the information and documentation requested have not been provided," it read.The letter included eight pages containing 42 questions covering a number of issues, from the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) private investment, to the Fifa Peace Prize and the controversial suspended ban given to USA striker Folarin Balogun at the World Cup."The withdrawal of FFE, the acknowledgement of mistakes and the announcement of 'potential governance reforms' do not answer how the relevant decisions were taken or why the Fifa Council was not involved at the appropriate stage," it continued."Any refusal to disclose information or documents should be justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon."These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the Fifa Council - nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them."Uefa did not outline what steps it intended to take should Fifa not meet the deadline, but will hope it adds to the pressure on Infantino ahead of November 18, the cut-off date for any candidates to confirm they are standing against him in next year's presidential election. The questions were first put to Infantino at the Fifa Council last week, with Infantino then asking that they were submitted in writing. Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that "if he doesn't answer those questions, he's not fit to be Fifa president".Fifa has been approached for comment. Uefa has posed a great number of questions about FFE."When was the idea of FFE first explored, by whom and with what objective?" Uefa asked. "Who within Fifa authorised the development of the project, and which members of the Fifa administration were involved?"What concrete measures will Fifa put in place to ensure that the shortcomings identified in the FFE process cannot occur again in the future?"Uefa goes on to ask about the circumstances surrounding Infantino's initial presentation of the FFE plan to senior Fifa executives. In particular, it raises a question about a potential investigation into Fifa in the United States. BBC Sport has approached Uefa to ascertain what this is in relation to."According to information received from several sources, two days before the vote by the bureau of the management board on the FFE proposal, the Fifa president informed members of the management board that the US authorities were investigating Fifa's administration," Uefa claim. "Can he confirm whether such a statement was made and, if so, explain the information on which it was based, the reasons for raising it at that particular moment and whether he considered the potential pressure it might place on members immediately before their decision on FFE?"Uefa requested information on whether Infantino would have held or expected to hold any position, role or function in FFE, either during or following his tenure as Fifa president.The relationship with Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital was covered in detail, asking why an agreement granting exclusivity to the company was signed without prior consultation of the Fifa Council."Why was Thrive Capital selected as lead investor, without any competitive tendering process and under conditions of strict confidentiality, despite its links to the family of the recipient of the Fifa Peace Prize?" Uefa asked.Kushner is the brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law, while the US president was awarded the Peace Prize.Uefa also requested answer about the award of the Peace Prize, specifically who decided to establish it, for what purpose, and who decided that Trump should receive it.When the FFE plan was revealed in the days following the World Cup final, Infantino told the 211 member associations (MAs) they would receive $40m (£30m) if they backed it. He then set a deadline of 19 September for federations to accept his plans if they wanted to access an initial $20m (£15m).However, once the scheme was abandoned, Uefa and Concacaf called on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the MAs and, last week, Infantino agreed, proposing to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn).The releasing of cash from its reserves will result in double the level of planned distribution funding for MAs from 2027 to 2030, with $25m (£19m) available per member association."Why was substantially increased funding for MAs presented in connection with FFE and external investment, rather than being financed directly from Fifa's own resources?" Uefa has asked."Given Fifa's strong financial position, why was it considered necessary to seek investment from private investors? What financial or strategic advantages would such an arrangement have offered compared with funding football development directly from Fifa's own resources, particularly in light of Fifa's subsequent proposal to do precisely that on a substantially increased scale?"While Fifa is yet to respond, sources have indicated its ability to answer certain questions are restricted by the legal action that Uefa has launched. Last month, it filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.Infantino has faced intense scrutiny over the case of Balogun, who avoided an immediate suspension after being sent off at the World Cup.Balogun's ban was lifted by Fifa's disciplinary committee, after US President Donald Trump asked Infantino for the decision to be reviewed.Fifa insisted the committee was independent but its legal committee is now reviewing a proposal to amend its disciplinary code, which would prevent a repeat, with an update due in December. Uefa has asked why this is necessary."President Trump publicly acknowledged having called the Fifa president to request a review of the Balogun disciplinary case. What exactly did he ask him to do, and what was his response?", Uefa has asked. "Would the case have been reviewed in the absence of his intervention?""Following that conversation, did the Fifa president or the Fifa secretary general communicate with anyone within Fifa, including members of the administration or the chair of the disciplinary committee, concerning the Balogun case? If so, could Fifa specify with whom, when and the nature of those communications? "We also request all correspondence and other communications concerning the case between the chair of the disciplinary committee and the Fifa administration, including the Fifa president and Fifa's chief legal officer."Could Fifa provide the full written reasons for the decision in the Balogun case, including the information and evidence before the disciplinary committee? "Who decided that the matter should be determined by a single member of the committee, on what basis…and what were the exceptional circumstances relied upon to justify the decision?"Uefa also asked why no disciplinary action was taken against DR Congo after the African nation reportedly played an ineligible player in World Cup qualifying. Usually, this would result in the country being disqualified but no action was taken.Reports in the lead-up last week's Fifa Council suggested Infantino had received an additional salary from Fifa's US World Cup organising entity (FWC2026 US Inc.) which was not disclosed in Fifa's annual report.Uefa has asked Fifa to "clarify the nature, amount and basis of these payments, why they were not disclosed and whether they were reviewed and approved by the competent Fifa bodies."It added: "Could Fifa also confirm whether the additional remuneration was treated as taxable income and whether the corresponding income tax was paid?"Fifa has previously denied paying Infantino a second salary, and insisted it complies with all reporting requirements in relation to compensation, saying it "strongly rejects any claims that it has failed to disclose any financial information and has violated Fifa's statutes."Uefa also asked about reported "advanced discussions involving the US president and individuals associated with him concerning a Fifa cryptocurrency", and the $75m (£56.3m) investment in Palestine via Trump's Board of Peace.The extended 27-minute half-time interval during the World Cup final and introduction of mandatory hydration breaks were also raised.Uefa wanted answers on the "seven-year, $4m (£3m) lease of office premises in Trump Tower, New York, involving Eric Trump, for premises reportedly unused for much of the year".It wrote: "These matters, taken together, raise questions that extend beyond the ordinary institutional relationship between Fifa and the government of a World Cup host country."Could Fifa provide a detailed explanation of these arrangements and interventions, including the decision-making processes followed, the identification and management of any potential conflicts of interest, the financial implications for Fifa and the extent to which the competent Fifa bodies were informed or consulted?"Also brought up was the impartiality of the chair of the Fifa electoral committee before next year's presidential election who, Uefa says, "attended the entire 2026 World Cup as an accredited individual, with his expenses covered by Fifa for more than five weeks".It also asked for a full list of the guests seated in the VIP and VVIP sections "including their names, positions and the reasons for their invitations".

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Uefa gives Fifa deadline to release key documents

title: Tommy Robinson 'intimidated' Daily Mail reporters, trial hears
description: Political activist Tommy Robinson used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten two Daily Mail journalists, forcing them to employ security or le
body: Political activist Tommy Robinson used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten two Daily Mail journalists, forcing them to employ security or leave home, a court has heard.The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence towards reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber.Opening the trial, prosecutor Ben Holt said the case was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to what he perceived to be "an unnecessary intrusion into his holiday" in the aftermath of the 2024 Southport attacks.Robinson, who founded the English Defence League, entered not guilty pleas to the charges in July last year.Holt said Dirnhuber had to move house because of the alleged harassment, while Young was given a close protection officer by the Daily Mail after photographs of his wife and children were posted on Robinson's X account.The judge at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Justice Cavanagh, told the jury: "This is not a trial about or an assessment of the defendant's political views."Ben Holt, for the prosecution, described Yaxley-Lennon as a "well-known public figure" with a "large, vocal online following" that now included more than two million followers on social media website X.Robinson posted on X before the trial began to thank the social media platform's owner Elon Musk for funding his case – and said his court fees to date had cost him £400,000.Holt said that after the murders of three young girls in Southport on 29 July 2024, Yaxley-Lennon made a number of posts on social media. This alerted the Daily Mail and Mail Online to the fact that he was in Cyprus.The Daily Mail published articles that included photographs of the defendant, including one showing him "reclining on a sunbed using his mobile telephone".Southwark Crown Court heard that over the following days, he made a series of posts on his X account in response.On 4 August, these included: "The daily mail have purposely gave the location of where I am with my children knowing full well that people want to kill me."Another post said: "The daily mail have purposely doxed the exact location of my family. How can they be allowed to do this'."There were no identifiable pictures of Yaxley-Lennon's children published by the Daily Mail or in the Mail Online, jurors were told.Holt said the trial was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to the articles, and accused him of using "bully-boy tactics" to "intimidate" the journalists."He chose to frighten them, arrange for individuals to go to their addresses," said the prosecuting counsel."On social media — to millions of followers — he circulated images of their homes. "His supporters got involved — threatening the journalists. "Understandably, you might agree, they were scared; in some circumstances, being forced to leave their homes."The court heard that on 5 August, Dirnhuber received a number of direct messages from Robinson/Yaxley-Lennon.These included "you have endangered my children", "I'll be knocking at your door," and "let your bosses know I'm coming to all of your houses".The jury panel also heard details of an alleged phone conversation between Yaxley-Lennon and Young."He said that he had Mr Young's telephone number. He recited his home address," Mr Holt told jurors.Yaxley-Lennon then became, according to Mr Young, "increasingly menacing".The prosecutor continued: "He raised his voice, he was swearing and shouting."He said that he had been researching Mr Young's family and threatened to publish photographs of them and their addresses online."Mr Lennon told Mr Young that he would be coming to Mr Young's house and he would have to move house."He was going to shove a camera in his face and ask questions. "Mr Young told him that he did not want to engage with him — all complaints should be directed to the Daily Mail legal department."Mr Young believes Mr Lennon said 'I'm coming to get you'."

schema.headline: Tommy Robinson 'intimidated' Daily Mail reporters, trial hears

title: Tottenham v Coventry City: How the players rated
description: Antonin Kinsky: Fumbled first-half corner and not great with his feet. 5Tosin Adarabioyo: Powerful in the air and did well in the physical challenges
body: Antonin Kinsky: Fumbled first-half corner and not great with his feet. 5Tosin Adarabioyo: Powerful in the air and did well in the physical challenges until he went off injured. 6Jan Paul van Hecke: Disappointing night. Uncertain moments and lost possession for Coventry City's goal, but did make one brave clearance. 5Micky van de Ven: Superb tackle to stop Brandon Thomas-Asante in the first half and solid all-round display. 7Archie Gray: Busy and did his best to give Spurs some creative edge. 6Sandro Tonali: Occasional flashes but still struggles to justify his £100m price tag. Needs to produce more. 6James Maddison: Brilliant strike on his first start for 18 months. Always prompting and probing. Revelled in his return to the starting line-up until understandably tiring. 8Andrew Robertson: Some trademark surging runs and always willing to join the attack but picked up an injury. 6Mohammed Kudus: Mixed night. Some good things but too often short of end product. 5Omar Marmoush: Had struggled but then scored a superb goal. 6Dominic Solanke: Tireless but little luck. Booked and had a shot on the turn over in first half. 5Subs:Conor Gallagher (on 69, Maddison): Not able to get into the game. 5Mateus Fernandes (on 69, Tosin): Little impact. 5Ben Davies (on 69, Robertson): Experienced head to close out the win and got himself a goal. 6Mathys Tel (on 87 Marmoush).Dejan Kulusevski (on 87 Kudus).Subs not used: Dubravka, Senesi, Olusesi, Williams-Barnett.Carl Rushworth: No chance with first two goals but a horror show for the third from Ben Davies. 5Milan van Ewijk: Long throws a threat, especially in the first half. Caught an elbow when trying to challenge Marmoush for his goal. 6Bobby Thomas: Vital headed clearance and tower of strength in defence. 7Ethan Pinnock: Another dependable performance as Coventry looked solid and well-organised at the back. 6Jay Dasilva: Quiet night. Booked for challenge on Kudus. 5Caleb Yirenkyi: Not able to exert much influence and was substituted. Booked for a poor challenge on Gray. 5Matt Grimes: Always busy but not able to have a significant impact. 5Brandon Thomas-Asante: Industrious and was only denied a goal by Van de Ven's superb first-half tackle. 6Jack Rudoni: Showed great determination to bustle his way through for his goal. 7Tatsuhiro Sakamoto: Some dangerous deliveries and had a good chance in the first half. 6Sidiki Cherif: Some nice lay-offs and full of effort. Hurt his shoulder in an awkward fall. 6Subs:Frank Onyeka (on, 60 Yirenkyi): No effect. 5Taiwo Awoniyi (on 60, Cherif): Bustling but unable to provide threat. 5Ephron Mason-Clark (on 78, Thomas-Asante).Gustavo Hamer (on 78, Sakamoto).Kaine Kesler-Hayden (on 87, Rudoni).Subs not used: Bentley, Simms, Mfuni, Torp.

schema.headline: Tottenham v Coventry City: How the players rated

title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
description: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by
body: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.The Prime Minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly penalised. In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby. The charge was eventually dropped.Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies".Burnham, the prime minister, said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat."These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them."The new rules will give drivers:a guaranteed 5 minute period to decide whether to parkA 10 minute window to leave without facing a penaltyCancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, like vehicle breakdowns in car parksCancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machinesMaximum charges of £20 on appeal for slip-ups like forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parkingA freeze on the maximum parking charge at £100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of PracticeOperators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it far more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge. Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets. RAC analysis of government data showed a record 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025/2026 - a 17% increase from a year earlier.With each charge worth up to £100, the data, analysed by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation, suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day.The yellow and black envelope of a Penalty Charge Notice, or PCN, is a dreaded sight for motorists returning to their car.The AA has warned some drivers pay up even if they have nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle. It said people felt they would not get a fair hearing if they appealed fines, with many saying they feared legal action.The current private parking industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024.But the culture of motorists feeling they have been harshly penalised has spurred the government to present a formalised code to Parliament. The British Parking Association told the BBC it welcomed the changes, but said "many of the principles within the new framework are already reflected in the existing voluntary Code of Practice". The new Code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales after motorists said they wanted independent oversight of the private parking industry.Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said drivers "finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators". He said in the past they have "aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up".But the RAC's head of policy Simon Williams said it wasn't the leap his firm had been campaigning for. He called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of PCNs and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one.The government said it will be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendation from the Competition and Markets Authority.
